chapters.name: Chapter 1: How mobile money works, and using it safely

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Your wallet, your PIN and your phone
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set a strong PIN, lock your phone and name the people who must never get your PIN.
This lesson builds toward: Using your own phone and mobile money account, you will set a PIN that is hard to guess, lock your phone and keep the PIN to yourself, sharing the PIN with no one, not even family or someone who says they are staff.
A mobile money wallet is an account linked to your SIM card. You put cash in at an agent, send it, pay with it, and take it out again. Your PIN (personal identification number) is the key to the wallet. Anyone who has your phone and your PIN can empty it.
Choose a PIN that is hard to guess: not your birth year, not 1234 or 0000, not the last digits of your phone number. Cover the keypad when you type it at an agent or in a crowded matatu or market. Lock the phone itself with a PIN, pattern or fingerprint, and if your phone allows it, set a SIM PIN too, so a thief cannot put your SIM in another phone.
Never share your mobile money PIN or a one-time code with anyone: not a friend, not a child, not an agent, and not a caller who says they are from Safaricom, MTN, Orange or Wave. The providers say clearly that their staff will never ask for your PIN. If someone asks, it is a scam.
If your phone is lost or stolen, or your line suddenly stops working, call your provider at once from another phone to block the SIM and wallet. A line that dies without reason can be a SIM swap, where a criminal moves your number to their SIM.
Step by step:
- Change your PIN from the menu if it is easy to guess (birth year, 1234, repeated numbers).
- Set a screen lock on your phone.
- Turn on a SIM PIN if your phone offers it.
- Cover the keypad when you type your PIN.
- Write your provider's official help number on paper, not in a message from a stranger.
- If the phone is lost or the line dies, call the provider from another phone to block it.
Words to know:
- Wallet: your mobile money account, linked to your SIM card.
- PIN: personal identification number: the secret number that lets you use your wallet.
- SIM swap: when your phone number is moved to a new SIM card; criminals try this to take over your wallet.
Official sources:
- The Star, Kenya (27 March 2025): common fraud schemes targeting M-Pesa users; report on 333, Zuri or the app; Safaricom never asks for your PIN
- Ghana News Agency (October 2026): MTN cautions customers not to share their MoMo PIN
Try it now: Look at your own PIN in your head (do not write it down or tell anyone). Is it your birth year, 1234 or a repeated number? If yes, change it from the menu today. Then check that your phone has a screen lock.
You can now set a PIN that is hard to guess, lock your phone and SIM, and refuse anyone who asks for your PIN.

options: 1990, your birth year
A number with no link to your birthday or phone number
The last four digits of your phone number
check.why: A PIN with no link to facts about you is hard for others to guess.

check.q: A caller says he is from your mobile money provider and needs your PIN to fix your account. What do you do?
options: Hang up; real staff never ask for your PIN
Give the PIN, then change it later
Give only the first two digits
Send him the code from your phone instead
check.why: Providers never ask for your PIN or codes; anyone who does is a scammer.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Sending and paying: check the name before the PIN
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Check the name, number and amount on the confirmation screen before you enter your PIN.
This lesson builds toward: When you send money, pay a merchant or use an agent, you will check the recipient's name, the number and the amount on the confirmation screen before you enter your PIN, and keep the confirmation message, every time, and stopping if anything does not match.
Most mistakes and many scams can be stopped in one place: the confirmation screen. Before you type your PIN, your phone shows who you are paying and how much. In Kenya, M-Pesa shows the name for a number, till or Paybill; other providers show a name or merchant name too.
Read it slowly. Is it the right person or shop? Is the amount right? 5,000 is not 50,000. When paying a shop, check the till, merchant or Paybill number from a sign or receipt in the shop, not from a number someone sends you.
If the name is wrong or strange, cancel. Do not enter your PIN "to see what happens". After you pay, keep the confirmation message (SMS) until you are sure the person or shop got the money. It is your proof.
Example: Ama in Kumasi pays a supplier GHS 600 with MTN MoMo. The screen shows a different name from the supplier's. She cancels, calls the supplier on the number she already has, and finds she typed one digit wrong.
Step by step:
- Type the number, merchant code or till.
- Type the amount and read it twice.
- On the confirmation screen, read the name, number and amount.
- If anything does not match, cancel.
- If it all matches, cover the keypad and type your PIN.
- Keep the confirmation SMS as proof.
Words to know:
- Confirmation screen: the screen that shows who you are paying and how much, before you enter your PIN.
- Till / merchant code / Paybill: numbers that shops and companies use to receive payments.
- Confirmation SMS: the message your provider sends after a payment; your proof.
Official sources:
- Citizen Digital, Kenya: how to reverse an M-Pesa payment (forward the confirmation SMS to 456; wrong till or Paybill: call 100)
Try it now: Next time you send money or pay, stop on the confirmation screen and say the name, number and amount out loud before you type your PIN. Then find the confirmation SMS and do not delete it.
You can now check the name, number and amount before you enter your PIN, and keep the confirmation message as proof.

check.q: The confirmation screen shows a name you do not know. What do you do?
options: Enter the PIN; names are often wrong
Enter the PIN and ask later
Send a smaller amount first
Cancel and check the number with the person
check.why: A strange name means a wrong number or a trick; cancel before the PIN.

check.q: Why keep the confirmation SMS after paying?
options: It is your proof if something goes wrong
It earns you points
The law says delete it
It makes the next payment cheaper
check.why: The confirmation message proves the payment and is needed for a reversal or complaint.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Agents, fees and your records
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Read the fee for a transaction from your provider's official tariff and do a safe cash-out at an agent.
This lesson builds toward: When you send money, pay a merchant or use an agent, you will check the recipient's name, the number and the amount on the confirmation screen before you enter your PIN, and keep the confirmation message, every time, and stopping if anything does not match. Using what you learned and your provider's official website or SIM pack, you will write a one-page mobile money safety plan for you or your family, covering PIN rules, the name check, official help channels, scam signs, first-hour steps and a monthly statement check.
An agent is a shop where you put cash into your wallet (cash in, or deposit) or take cash out (withdraw). Use a registered agent with the provider's sign and agent number. Do the transaction yourself on your own phone when you can, and count the cash before you leave.
Fees depend on the provider, the country, the amount and the type of transaction. Do not guess and do not trust a fee someone tells you. Read the official tariff on the provider's website or app, in the shop, or by dialing the menu. Many apps also show the fee before you confirm. Sending to someone on another network or to a bank may cost more.
A fake agent may say "give me your phone, I will do it for you", or ask for your PIN. Never hand over your phone with the PIN. Real agents do not need it.
Once a month, read your mini statement or full statement from the menu or app. Look for payments you do not recognise. Example: Moussa, a tailor in Dakar, checks his Wave history every month-end and writes his total sent and total received in a notebook. Figures in this course are examples only.
Step by step:
- Find the official fee table on the provider's website, app or shop poster.
- Look up the fee for the amount you want to send or withdraw.
- At the agent, check the sign and agent number.
- Start the withdrawal on your own phone; check the agent's name on screen.
- Count the cash before you leave.
- Read your statement once a month.
Words to know:
- Agent: a registered shop that does cash in and cash out for a mobile money provider.
- Tariff: the official table of fees for each type and size of transaction.
- Mini statement: a short list of your last few transactions, from the menu or app.
Official sources:
- Central Bank of Kenya (regulates mobile money and lists licensed payment service providers)
- BCEAO, Central Bank of West African States: electronic money institutions (XOF countries such as Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire)
Try it now: Find your provider's official fee table (website, app or shop poster). Write down the fee for sending one amount you often send, for example KES 1,000, NGN 5,000, GHS 100 or XOF 10,000. Then open your mini statement and check every line.
You can now read the real fee from the official tariff, use an agent safely and check your statement for strange payments.

check.q: At the agent, the agent asks for your phone and PIN to "make it faster". What do you do?
options: Give them; agents are trusted
Give the phone but not the PIN
Do it yourself and keep your PIN private
Write the PIN on paper for the agent
check.why: Real agents never need your PIN; you start and confirm the transaction yourself.

check.q: Where do you find the real fee for a transfer?
options: What a stranger tells you
The provider's official tariff, app or shop poster
A WhatsApp forward
Your neighbour's guess
check.why: Fees change and differ by country, so read them on official channels.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Scams, mistakes and your safety plan

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Spotting mobile money scams
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Identify the six common mobile money scams and the warning sign in each.
This lesson builds toward: Given six calls or messages about mobile money, you will identify which ones are scams and name the warning sign in each, getting at least 5 of 6 right.
Scammers use calls, SMS, WhatsApp and social media. They pretend to be your provider, a relative, an agent, a buyer or a company with a job. The tricks change, but the warning signs stay the same.
1. Fake reversal: you get an SMS that looks like a payment to you, then a call: "I sent you money by mistake, please send it back." Check your real balance first. Often no money arrived; the SMS came from an ordinary phone number, not the provider. 2. PIN or code request: anyone who asks for your PIN or a one-time code. 3. Fake staff: "Your account will be blocked unless you dial this code or tell us your details." 4. Prize or promotion: "You won, send a fee to receive your prize." 5. Fake job or loan: an offer that asks you to pay a fee first. 6. Urgent family message: "Mum, I am in trouble, send money to this new number."
Real messages from the provider come from its official name or short code, not an ordinary mobile number. Providers do not ask you to dial codes to fix your account or win a prize. If something feels urgent, stop. Call the person or the provider back on a number you already know.
Example: Chinedu in Enugu gets an SMS saying NGN 20,000 arrived, then a call asking him to send it back. He checks his balance in the app: nothing arrived. He hangs up and reports the number.
Step by step:
- Check the sender: official name or short code, or an ordinary number?
- Check your real balance in the menu or app.
- Ask: are they asking for my PIN, a code, a fee, or speed?
- Stop and call back on a number you already know.
- Report the scam number to your provider.
Words to know:
- Fake reversal: a trick where someone pretends they sent you money by mistake and asks you to send it back.
- One-time code (OTP): a short code sent to your phone to confirm an action; never share it.
- Short code: the short official number a provider sends messages from.
Official sources:
- The Star, Kenya (27 March 2025): common fraud schemes targeting M-Pesa users; report on 333, Zuri or the app; Safaricom never asks for your PIN
- Ghana News Agency (October 2026): MTN cautions customers not to share their MoMo PIN
Try it now: Look through your SMS inbox for messages about money. For each one, decide: official short code or ordinary number? Does it ask for a PIN, code, fee or speed? Write down any scam signs you find.
You can now spot the six common mobile money scams and say the warning sign in each.

check.q: An SMS from an ordinary mobile number says you received XAF 25,000. Then a caller asks you to send it back. What do you do first?
options: Send it back quickly to be honest
Check your real balance in the menu or app
Give the caller your PIN to reverse it
Forward the SMS to friends
check.why: Fake reversal SMS come from ordinary numbers; your real balance shows the truth.

check.q: A message says you won a phone and must pay a delivery fee first. What is the warning sign?
options: It mentions a phone
It came in the evening
It asks you to pay a fee to get a prize
It uses your first name
check.why: Real prizes do not need a fee first; paying to receive is a classic scam.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Wrong send or fraud: the first hour
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Report a wrong send or a fraud through your provider's official channels the same day.
This lesson builds toward: After money goes to the wrong number or you suspect fraud, you will report it through your provider's official channels and follow the reversal steps, the same day, keeping the original confirmation message and using no number given by a stranger.
Act fast. A reversal is easier while the money is still in the other wallet. Keep the original confirmation SMS; do not delete or edit it.
Use only official channels: the help line printed on your SIM pack or the provider's website, the official app, the official short code, or a provider shop. Never use a number from a stranger or a social media comment, and never pay anyone who offers to "recover" your money for a fee.
Example from Kenya: Safaricom's published channels include forwarding the M-Pesa confirmation SMS to 456 to ask for a reversal to the wrong person, calling 100 for a wrong till or Paybill, and forwarding a fraud number or message to 333. Other providers have their own steps; read them on the provider's official website or app, because numbers and steps change.
A reversal is not guaranteed. If the person has already withdrawn the money and refuses to return it, the provider may tell you to go to the police. If your PIN or line was stolen, report to the provider first, then the police. If the provider does not solve it, the central bank has a consumer complaints process (for example the Central Bank of Nigeria or the Bank of Ghana).
Step by step:
- Do not delete the confirmation SMS.
- Within the hour, use your provider's official reversal or fraud channel.
- Note the date, time, amount, transaction ID and who you spoke to.
- If the PIN or line was stolen, block the SIM and wallet first.
- If needed, report to the police with the SMS.
- If the provider does not solve it, use the central bank's complaints process.
Words to know:
- Reversal: when the provider returns money sent to the wrong number, if it is still there.
- Transaction ID: the code in the confirmation SMS that identifies one payment.
- Recovery scam: a fake offer to get your lost money back if you pay a fee.
Official sources:
- Citizen Digital, Kenya: how to reverse an M-Pesa payment (forward the confirmation SMS to 456; wrong till or Paybill: call 100)
- The Star, Kenya (27 March 2025): common fraud schemes targeting M-Pesa users; report on 333, Zuri or the app; Safaricom never asks for your PIN
- Central Bank of Nigeria: consumer protection
- Bank of Ghana: complaints procedures and the list of licensed institutions
Try it now: Find your own provider's official reversal and fraud steps on its website, app or SIM pack. Write them on paper: the number or code, and what to send. Do not copy them from a WhatsApp forward.
You can now act within the first hour after a wrong send or fraud, using only your provider's official channels.

check.q: You sent money to the wrong number. What do you keep?
options: Nothing; delete the SMS
Only the amount in your head
A screenshot from a stranger
The original confirmation SMS
check.why: The original confirmation message has the transaction ID the provider needs.

check.q: Someone on Facebook offers to recover your lost money for a small fee. What is this?
options: A recovery scam; use only official channels
A helpful service
The central bank's process
A provider shop
check.why: Paying a stranger to recover money is a second scam; official channels are free.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Your mobile money safety plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a one-page mobile money safety plan for you or your family.
This lesson builds toward: Using what you learned and your provider's official website or SIM pack, you will write a one-page mobile money safety plan for you or your family, covering PIN rules, the name check, official help channels, scam signs, first-hour steps and a monthly statement check.
A safety plan puts everything from this course on one page, so you and your family know what to do before something goes wrong. Keep it on paper at home, not only on the phone.
It has six parts: 1. PIN and phone rules (hard PIN, screen lock, SIM PIN, never share). 2. The name check before every PIN. 3. Your provider's official help and fraud channels, copied from its website, app or SIM pack. 4. The six scam warning signs. 5. The first-hour steps after a wrong send or fraud. 6. A monthly statement check, with a date.
Talk it through with older parents and teenagers, who are often targeted. Agree a family rule: "We never send money to a new number because of an urgent message. We call back on the old number first."
Example: Fatima, a trader in Casablanca, keeps her plan inside her cash book. Each month-end she checks her wallet history and ticks the date on the plan.
Step by step:
- Write your PIN and phone-lock rules.
- Write the name-check rule.
- Copy your provider's official help and fraud channels from an official source.
- List the six scam warning signs.
- Write your first-hour steps.
- Set a monthly date to check your statement.
- Read it with your family.
Words to know:
- Safety plan: a short written list of rules and steps that protect your money.
Official sources:
- Central Bank of Kenya (regulates mobile money and lists licensed payment service providers)
- Bank of Ghana: complaints procedures and the list of licensed institutions
- BCEAO, Central Bank of West African States: electronic money institutions (XOF countries such as Senegal and Côte d'Ivoire)
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page mobile money safety plan with all six parts. Copy your provider's help and fraud channels from its official website, app or SIM pack. Read it with one family member.
You can now write and share a mobile money safety plan that protects you and your family.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds PIN and phone rules No PIN rules, or the plan contains a real PIN or code. Says: hard-to-guess PIN, screen lock, never share the PIN or codes, block at once if the phone is lost. Also includes a SIM PIN and what to do if the line suddenly dies (possible SIM swap). Name check No step to check before the PIN. Says to check the name, number and amount on the confirmation screen and keep the confirmation SMS. Adds taking till or merchant codes only from the shop itself and calling back on a known number about "new" payment numbers. Scam warning signs Fewer than four scam signs, or vague ones. Lists the six common scams with a warning sign for each. Adds a real example the learner or family has seen and how they spotted it. Official channels and first hour Help numbers missing, or copied from an unofficial source. Gives the provider's official help, reversal and fraud channels (from the website, app or SIM pack) and first-hour steps. Also names the central bank complaints route and the police step, and says where each channel was copied from. Monthly check and sharing No regular check, and the plan is not shared. Sets a monthly statement check and the plan was read with one family member. Includes a family call-back rule and a first check already done and dated. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Where should the help numbers in your plan come from?
options: A WhatsApp forward
The provider's official website, app or SIM pack
A caller who says he is staff
A social media comment
check.why: Scammers spread fake help numbers; copy them from official sources only.

check.q: Which family rule protects against the urgent-message scam?
options: Always send fast in an emergency
Share one PIN for the whole family
Reply with your PIN to prove it is you
Call back on the person's old number before sending
check.why: Calling back on a known number shows whether the urgent message is real.
